Here there are two issues.

This view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Muqatil and al-Suddi. Then among those who hold this view, some say it is an oath by the fish upon whose back the earth rests, and it is in a sea beneath the lowest earth. Others say it is an oath by the fish that held Yunus (peace be upon him) in its belly. Others say it is an oath by the fish whose blood stained the arrow of Namrud.

The second view, also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and preferred by al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Qatadah, is that the nun is the inkwell (dawah). From it is the saying of the poet:

When longing draws me back to them, the nun pours forth tears in flowing streams.

In that case this is an oath by the inkwell and the pen, since the benefit of both through writing is great, for mutual understanding is sometimes achieved by speech and sometimes sought through writing.

The third view: that the nun is a tablet on which the angels write what Allah commands them, narrated by Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah as a marfu' report.

The fourth view: that the nun is the ink with which the angels write. Know that these views are weak, because if we take it as something sworn by, then if it is a common noun it should be in the genitive with tanwin, since the oath on this assumption would be by an indefinite inkwell or an indefinite fish, as if it were said: "By a fish and the pen," or "By an inkwell and the pen." And if it is a proper noun, we should either treat it as triptote and put it in the genitive, or if we treat it as diptote, leave it without tanwin and put it in the accusative.

The fifth view: that the nun here is the last letter of al-Rahman, for from al-Rahman the letter n is combined to form the name al-Rahman, so Allah mentioned this last letter of this name, and the intent is an oath by the complete name. This too is weak, because permitting it opens the door to the nonsense of the Batiniyyah. Rather, the truth is that it is either the name of the surah, or its purpose is a challenge, or the other views mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The second issue: The reciters differ regarding the clear pronunciation and the concealment of the nun in His saying ﴿Nun, and the pen﴾. Whoever pronounces it clearly does so because he intends a pause on it, as shown by the meeting of two unvocalized letters in it. When it is paused upon, it is treated as separate from what follows, and when it is separate from what follows, clarity is required, because concealment occurs only with the letters of the mouth when they are joined. Since the hamzah is not elided with them, we know they are treated as joined, and when you join them you conceal the nun. We have mentioned this in (Ta-Sin) and (Ya-Sin). Al-Farra' said: clear pronunciation is more pleasing to me, because it is a spelling-out of letters (hija'), and spelling-out is like something paused upon, even when joined.

* His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And the pen﴾ has two views:

One: that the oath by it is the genus, applying to every pen with which whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth writes. He, Exalted, says: ﴿And your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know﴾ (al-'Alaq: 3–5). So He bestowed favor by making writing easy with the pen just as He bestowed it with speech, saying: ﴿He created man, taught him eloquence﴾ (al-Rahman: 3–4). The benefit of it is that it makes the absent present, so a person can define the distant through it just as he can define the near through speech.

The second: that the sworn-by pen is the specific known pen that appears in the report, "that the first thing Allah created was the pen." Ibn 'Abbas said: the first thing Allah created was the pen, then He said to it: write what will occur until the Hour is established, so it ran with what will occur until the Hour is established, of lifespans and deeds. He said: it is a pen of light whose length is as the distance between the heaven and the earth. Mujahid narrated from him that he said: the first thing Allah created was the pen, and He said: write the decree, so it wrote what will occur until the Day of Resurrection, and people only act upon a matter that has already been completed. The judge (al-Qadi) said: this report must be interpreted figuratively, because the pen, which is a specific instrument for writing, cannot be a living rational being that is commanded and forbidden. For combining being a responsible animal with being an instrument of writing is impossible. Rather, the intended meaning is that Allah, Exalted, set it in motion with everything that will happen, like His saying: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it "Be," and it is﴾ (Ghafir: 68), for there is no command or obligation there, but merely the execution of power over what is decreed without contest or resistance. It may also mean the thing inscribed and written. On both readings, if we take the pen as every pen among God's creatures, the meaning is clear, as though He, Exalted, swore by every pen and by everything that is written with every pen. It was said: rather, the intended meaning is what the guardian angels and the noble scribes inscribe. The pen may also be taken to mean its owners, so the pronoun in ﴿they inscribe﴾ refers to them, as though it were said: "and the owners of the pen and their inscribing," i.e., and what they write.

As for taking the pen as that specific pen, then the intended meaning of His saying ﴿and what they inscribe﴾ may be: and what they inscribe in it, which is the Preserved Tablet. The plural form in ﴿they inscribe﴾ is not intended to denote plurality but glorification. Or the intended meaning may be those things that were inscribed in it of deeds and lifespans and all matters that will occur until the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 68, verses 3–4:

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the thing sworn by, He followed it with mention of the thing sworn to, and said:

﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman﴾ ﴿and indeed for you is a reward never cut off﴾ ﴿and indeed you are upon a magnificent character﴾

Know that His saying: ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman﴾ contains two issues.

The first issue: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that "he (peace be upon him) withdrew from Khadijah to Hira', and she sought him but did not find him. Then he appeared to her with his face changed and without dust. She said to him: 'What is wrong with you?' So he mentioned the descent of Jibril (peace be upon him) and that he said to him: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ (al-'Alaq: 1), which is the first thing revealed of the Qur'an. He said: Then he brought me down to the lowest part of the earth, and he performed ablution and I performed ablution, then he prayed and I prayed with him two rak'ahs, and he said: 'This is the prayer, O Muhammad.' So the Prophet (peace be upon him) related that to Khadijah, and Khadijah went to Waraqah ibn Nawfal, who was her cousin, and he had abandoned the religion of his people and entered Christianity. She asked him, and he said: 'Send me Muhammad.' So she sent him, and he came to him and said to him: 'Has Jibril (peace be upon him) commanded you to call anyone to Allah?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'By Allah, if I live to your call, I will surely support you with a mighty support.' Then he died before the Messenger's call. That incident was spread on the tongues of the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they said: 'Indeed he is a madman.' So Allah, exalted is He, swore that he is not a madman, and that is the five verses at the beginning of this surah." Then Ibn 'Abbas said: The first thing revealed was His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ (al-A'la: 1), and this verse is the second.

The second issue: al-Zajjaj said: "Ant" (أنت) is the subject of "ma" (ما), and "bi-majnun" (بِمَجْنُونٍ) is the predicate, and His saying: ﴿by the grace of your Lord﴾ is a phrase inserted in between. The meaning is: madness has been removed from you by the grace of your Lord, just as it is said: "You are, by the praise of Allah, sensible," "You are, by the praise of Allah, not mad," "You are, by the grace of Allah, understanding," "You are, by the grace of Allah, not poor." Its meaning is that the praiseworthy attribute was obtained, and the blameworthy attribute was removed, only through the bounty, kindness and honour of Allah. 'Ata' and Ibn 'Abbas said: He means by the grace of your Lord upon you, through faith and prophethood. This is a reply to their saying: ﴿And they say: O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are a madman﴾ (al-Hijr: 6). Know that He, exalted is He, described him here with three kinds of attributes.

The first attribute: the negation of madness from him. Then, Allah, exalted is He, joined to this claim what serves as a conclusive proof of its truth. That is because His saying: ﴿by the grace of your Lord﴾ indicates that the favours of Allah, exalted is He, were manifest in his case: complete eloquence, perfect intellect, a pleasing conduct, freedom from every defect, and possession of every noble quality. When these favours are perceptible and manifest, their existence contradicts the occurrence of madness. Allah, exalted is He, drew attention to this subtle point so that it would serve as a certain proof that they were lying in their saying to him that he is mad.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿and indeed for you is a reward never cut off﴾. Regarding "al-mamnun" there are two views:

One of them, which is the view of most scholars, is that the meaning is: not diminished and not cut off. It is said: "manna-hu al-sayr," meaning it weakened him, and "al-manin" is the weak one; and "manna al-shay'" when he cut it off. From this is the saying of Labid:

"Grey, hunting (dogs), whose food is not cut off"

describing hunting dogs. A similar usage is His saying: ﴿a gift not cut off﴾ (Hud: 108).

The second view, which is the view of Mujahid, Muqatil and al-Kalbi, is that it is not restricted for you by way of obligation. The Mu'tazilah, in establishing this interpretation, said: it is not bestowed upon you as a favour, because it is a reward that you deserve for your action, and not a grace granted from the outset. But the first view is more fitting, because describing it as a reward indicates that there is no obligation in it, so reading it according to this meaning would be a repetition. Then they differed as to upon what this reward was obtained. Some people said: its meaning is that for you, in return for bearing this slander and foul speech, is a great and lasting reward. Others said: what is meant is that for you, in the manifestation of prophethood and miracles, in calling creatures to Allah, and in explaining the Law to them, is this pure and lasting reward. So their attributing madness to you should not prevent you from occupying yourself with this great matter, for by means of it you have a lofty station with Allah.

The third attribute: His saying: ﴿and indeed you are upon a magnificent character﴾. Concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that this is like an explanation of His earlier saying: ﴿by the grace of your Lord﴾, and a clarification to whoever accused him of madness that this is a lie and an error. That is because praiseworthy morals and pleasing actions were manifest from him, and one who is described by those morals and actions may not be attributed with madness, since the morals of madmen are evil. And since his praiseworthy morals were perfect, there is no doubt that Allah described them as magnificent. For this reason He said: ﴿Say: I do not ask of you any reward for it, and I am not of the pretenders﴾ (Sad: 86), i.e., I am not affected in what appears to you of my morals, because one who affects something does not sustain it for long, but it returns to his natural disposition. Others said: He described his character as magnificent only because He, exalted is He, said to him: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ (al-An'am: 90). This guidance which Allah commanded Muhammad to follow is not knowledge of Allah, because that would be imitation (taqlid), which is unfitting for the Messenger, nor is it the laws, because his law differs from their laws. So it is necessary that what is meant is his being commanded, peace be upon him, to follow each one of the earlier Prophets in what was specifically his of noble character. It is as if each of them was specialised in one kind, and when Muhammad, peace be upon him, was commanded to follow all of them, it was as if he was commanded with the totality of what was scattered among them. And since this was a lofty degree not attained by any prophet before him, Allah therefore described his character as magnificent. There is another subtle point in His saying: ﴿indeed you are upon a magnificent character﴾, for the word "upon" (على) indicates elevation, so the wording shows that he is elevated above these morals and in control of them, and that in relation to these beautiful morals he is like the master in relation to the servant, and like the commander in relation to the one commanded.

The second issue: Morality (khuluq, خُلُق) is a psychological disposition by which it becomes easy for its possessor to perform beautiful actions.

Know that performing beautiful actions is one thing, and the ease of performing them is another. The state by which that ease is obtained is the khuluq. Included in good character is guarding against avarice and miserliness, anger, and severity in dealings, endearing oneself to people by word and deed, abandoning severance and estrangement, leniency in contracts such as sale and others, and tolerance regarding the rights of one who has kinship or marital relation and has another right. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: its meaning is: "And indeed you are upon a magnificent religion." It is also narrated that Allah, exalted is He, said to him: "I have not created a religion more beloved to Me, nor more pleasing to Me, than this religion which I have chosen for you and for your community," meaning Islam. Know that this view is weak, because man has two powers: a theoretical power and a practical power,

and religion returns to the perfection of the theoretical power, while character returns to the perfection of the practical power, so it is not possible to read one as the other. It is also possible to answer this question in two ways:

The first way: that khuluq in the language is habit, whether that be in perception or in action.

The second way: we have explained that khuluq is the matter by which performing beautiful actions becomes easy. Since his holy spirit was intensely prepared for true divine knowledge and wholly unprepared to accept false beliefs, that ease was present in accepting true knowledge, so it is not far-fetched to call that ease by the name khuluq.

The third issue: Sa'id ibn Hisham said: "I said to 'A'ishah: 'Tell me about the character (khuluq) of the Messenger of Allah.' She said: 'Do you not recite the Qur'an?' I said: 'Yes.' She said: 'Indeed his character was the character of the Prophet (peace be upon him).'" And when she was asked another time, she said: "His character was the Qur'an," then she recited: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 1) up to ten verses. This is an indication that his blessed self was by nature drawn toward the unseen world and all that relates to it, and was by nature and by the demand of innate disposition strongly averse to bodily pleasures and worldly happiness. O Allah, grant us a portion of this state. Hisham ibn 'Urwah narrated from his father from 'A'ishah who said: "No one was better in character than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Whenever any of his companions or the people of his household called him, he would say: 'At your service (labbayk).'" Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed you are upon a magnificent character﴾. Anas said: "I served the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for ten years, and he never said to me regarding something I had done: 'Why did you do it?' nor regarding something I had not done: 'Why did you not do it?'" I say: Allah, exalted is He, described what relates to his theoretical power as magnificent, saying: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know, and the bounty of Allah upon you has been magnificent﴾ (al-Nisa': 113), and He described what relates to his practical power as magnificent, saying: ﴿And indeed you are upon a magnificent character﴾. Thus nothing remains for a human being beyond these two powers, and the combination of these two verses shows that his spirit among human spirits was magnificent and of lofty rank, as if, because of its strength and the intensity of its perfection, it was of the same kind as the spirits of the angels.

The Mu'tazilah, in establishing this interpretation, said: it is not bestowed upon you as a favour, because it is a reward that you deserve for your action, and not a grace granted from the outset. But the first view is more fitting, because describing it as a reward indicates that there is no obligation in it, so reading it according to this meaning would be a repetition. Then they differed as to upon what this reward was obtained. Some people said: its meaning is that for you, in return for bearing this slander and foul speech, is a great and lasting reward. Others said: what is meant is that for you, in the manifestation of prophethood and miracles, in calling creatures to Allah, and in explaining the Law to them, is this pure and lasting reward. The third attribute: His saying: ﴿and indeed you are upon a magnificent character﴾. Concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that this is like an explanation of His earlier saying: ﴿by the grace of your Lord﴾, and a clarification to whoever accused him of madness that this is a lie and an error. That is because praiseworthy morals and pleasing actions were manifest from him, and one who is described by those morals and actions may not be attributed with madness, since the morals of madmen are evil. And since his praiseworthy morals were perfect, there is no doubt that Allah described them as magnificent. For this reason He said: ﴿Say: I do not ask of you any reward for it, and I am not of the pretenders﴾ (Sad: 86), i.e., I am not affected in what appears to you of my morals, because one who affects something does not sustain it for long, but it returns to his natural disposition. Others said: He described his character as magnificent only because He, exalted is He, said to him: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ (al-An'am: 90). This guidance which Allah commanded Muhammad to follow is not knowledge of Allah, because that would be imitation (taqlid), which is unfitting for the Messenger, nor is it the laws, because his law differs from their laws. So it is necessary that what is meant is his being commanded, peace be upon him, to follow each one of the earlier Prophets in what was specifically his of noble character. It is as if each of them was specialised in one kind, and when Muhammad, peace be upon him, was commanded to follow all of them, it was as if he was commanded with the totality of what was scattered among them. And since this was a lofty degree not attained by any prophet before him, Allah therefore described his character as magnificent. There is another subtle point in His saying: ﴿indeed you are upon a magnificent character﴾, for the word "upon" (على) indicates elevation, so the wording shows that he is elevated above these morals and in control of them, and that in relation to these beautiful morals he is like the master in relation to the servant, and like the commander in relation to the one commanded.

The second issue: Morality (khuluq, خُلُق) is a psychological disposition by which it becomes easy for its possessor to perform beautiful actions.

Know that performing beautiful actions is one thing, and the ease of performing them is another. The state by which that ease is obtained is the khuluq. Included in good character is guarding against avarice and miserliness, anger, and severity in dealings, endearing oneself to people by word and deed, abandoning severance and estrangement, leniency in contracts such as sale and others, and tolerance regarding the rights of one who has kinship or marital relation and has another right. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: its meaning is: "And indeed you are upon a magnificent religion." It is also narrated that Allah, exalted is He, said to him: "I have not created a religion more beloved to Me, nor more pleasing to Me, than this religion which I have chosen for you and for your community," meaning Islam. Know that this view is weak, because man has two powers: a theoretical power and a practical power,

and religion returns to the perfection of the theoretical power, while character returns to the perfection of the practical power, so it is not possible to read one as the other. It is also possible to answer this question in two ways:

The first way: that khuluq in the language is habit, whether that be in perception or in action.

The second way: we have explained that khuluq is the matter by which performing beautiful actions becomes easy. Since his holy spirit was intensely prepared for true divine knowledge and wholly unprepared to accept false beliefs, that ease was present in accepting true knowledge, so it is not far-fetched to call that ease by the name khuluq.

The third issue: Sa'id ibn Hisham said: "I said to 'A'ishah: 'Tell me about the character (khuluq) of the Messenger of Allah.' She said: 'Do you not recite the Qur'an?' I said: 'Yes.' She said: 'Indeed his character was the character of the Prophet (peace be upon him).'" And when she was asked another time, she said: "His character was the Qur'an," then she recited: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 1) up to ten verses. This is an indication that his blessed self was by nature drawn toward the unseen world and all that relates to it, and was by nature and by the demand of innate disposition strongly averse to bodily pleasures and worldly happiness. O Allah, grant us a portion of this state. Hisham ibn 'Urwah narrated from his father from 'A'ishah who said: "No one was better in character than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Whenever any of his companions or the people of his household called him, he would say: 'At your service (labbayk).'" Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed you are upon a magnificent character﴾. Anas said: "I served the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for ten years, and he never said to me regarding something I had done: 'Why did you do it?' nor regarding something I had not done: 'Why did you not do it?'" I say: Allah, exalted is He, described what relates to his theoretical power as magnificent, saying: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know, and the bounty of Allah upon you has been magnificent﴾ (al-Nisa': 113), and He described what relates to his practical power as magnificent, saying: ﴿And indeed you are upon a magnificent character﴾. Thus nothing remains for a human being beyond these two powers, and the combination of these two verses shows that his spirit among human spirits was magnificent and of lofty rank, as if, because of its strength and the intensity of its perfection, it was of the same kind as the spirits of the angels.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 68, verses 5–7:**

﴿So you will see and they will see﴾, that is: so you will see, O Muhammad, and they will see, meaning the polytheists. And in this there are two opinions.

Among them are those who took this to refer to the affairs of this world, meaning: you will see and they will see in this world how the outcome of your affair and the outcome of theirs will be. You will become honoured in hearts, and they will become humiliated and cursed, and you will overpower them through killing and plunder. Muqatil said: this is a threat of punishment at Badr. Others took it to refer to the affairs of the Hereafter, and it is like His saying: ﴿They will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent one﴾ (al-Qamar: 26).

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿which of you is the afflicted one﴾,
there are several aspects (wujuh) to it:

The first, which is the view of al-Akhfash, Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba: the bi' (ba', the preposition) is a superfluous (silah za'ida) particle, and the meaning is "which of you is the afflicted one", i.e. the one afflicted with madness, like His saying: ﴿a tree that grows with oil﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 20), i.e. a tree that grows oil. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"We strike with the sword and hope with relief (bil-faraj)"

Al-Farra' criticised this answer and said: if the correct meaning can be expressed without dropping the ba', that is preferable. As for the verse of poetry, its meaning is: we hope to have what we are in removed by relief, or we hope for victory through relief.

The second, which is the choice of al-Farra' and al-Mubarrad: al-maftun here has the sense of al-futun, which is madness, and verbal nouns sometimes come in the form of the passive participle, such as al-ma'qud and al-maysur in the sense of al-'aqd (binding) and al-yusr (ease). It is said: "he has no ma'qud of opinion", i.e. no firm opinion. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and the narration of 'Atiyya from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: the ba' is in the sense of fi (in), and the meaning of the verse is: "you will see and they will see in which of the two groups is the madman: is it in the group of Islam or in the group of the disbelievers."

The fourth: al-maftun is Satan, for there is no doubt that he is afflicted in his religion. When they said "he is a madman," they were in effect saying "there is a devil in him." So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They will know tomorrow﴾ (al-Qamar: 26) with which of them is the devil whose touch produces madness and confusion of the intellect.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of those guided﴾. In this there are two aspects:

The first: the meaning is that your Lord is most knowing of the truly mad, who are those who strayed from His way, and He is most knowing of the sensible, who are the guided.

The second: the meaning is that they accused you of madness and described themselves as sensible, and they lied in that; rather, they are described by misguidance, while you are described by guidance. The distinction produced by guidance and misguidance is more worthy of consideration than the distinction produced by sanity and madness, because the fruit of that is eternal happiness (a) and wretchedness, whereas the fruit of this is happiness (a) and wretchedness in this world.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾. Know that when Allah the Exalted mentioned what the disbelievers did regarding the Messenger, and their attributing madness to him, despite the perfection Allah had granted him in religion and character, He followed this with what would urge him to be firm with his people, and He strengthened his heart with this despite the small number of his followers and the great number of the disbelievers. This surah is among the first to be revealed. So He said: ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾, meaning the leaders of the people of Makkah. This is because they invited him to the religion of his forefathers, and Allah forbade him to obey them. This is from Allah an incitement and stirring to firmness in opposing them.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿They wish you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾. ﴿And do not obey every oft-swearing contemptible one﴾ ﴿a slanderer, going about with gossip﴾ ﴿a hinderer of good, transgressing, sinful﴾ ﴿brutal, and after that, of doubtful lineage﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: al-Layth said: *al-idhhan* (compromise) is softness, flattery, and gentleness in speech. al-Mubarrad said: "Dahana al-rajul fi dinihi" and "dahana fi amrihi" mean he betrayed in it and showed the opposite of what he concealed. The meaning is: you would leave some of what you are upon, which they do not approve, to flatter them, so they would do the same and leave some of what you do not approve; you would be soft toward them and they would be soft toward you. And 'Ata reported from Ibn Abbas: "Law takfuru fa-yakfuruna" (if you disbelieved, they would disbelieve).

The second issue: ﴿fa-yudhinun﴾ is in the nominative and not in the subjunctive by the implied *an*, although it is the answer to the wish (*tamanni*); this is because it has been turned to another way, namely that it is made the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "fa-hum yudhinun" (so they compromise), like His saying: ﴿So whoever believes in his Lord, he fears no ...﴾ (al-Jinn: 13), meaning: "They wish you would compromise, so they compromise then." Sibawayh said: Harun, who was among the reciters, claimed that in some of the codices it reads: "Wadduu law tudhinu fa-yudhinu" (they wish you would compromise, so that they would compromise). Know that when He forbade him to obey the deniers, this includes forbidding obedience to all disbelievers, but He repeated the prohibition against obeying those among the disbelievers who were described with blameworthy qualities beyond disbelief. These qualities are the following:

The first quality: that he is *halaf* (an oft-swearer). The *halaf* is one who swears often, whether in truth or falsehood, and that is enough of a deterrent for one who is accustomed to swearing. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾ (al-Baqarah: 224).

The second quality: that he is *mahin* (contemptible). al-Zajjaj said: it is *fa'il* from *mahana* (contemptibility). Then there are two views:

One of them: that *mahana* is lowliness and insignificance in opinion and discernment.

The second: that he is contemptible because what is meant is one who swears falsely, and a liar is despised by people.

I say: that he is an oft-swearer indicates that he does not know the greatness and majesty of Allah the Exalted, for if he knew that, he would not have proceeded at every time and occasion, for the sake of every falsehood, to call upon His name and attributes as witness. And whoever does not know the greatness of Allah, and whose heart is attached to seeking the worldly life, is contemptible. This shows that dignity of self is attained only by one who recognizes his own servitude, and that its abasement is attained only by one who is heedless of the secret of servitude.

The third quality: that he is *hammaz*, which is the one who defames and reviles. al-Mubarrad said: the one who *yahmiz* people, i.e., reminds them of what is disliked, and the effect of that is revealing faults. It was reported from al-Hasan: he twists his cheeks at people's necks. I have already examined this matter at length in His saying: ﴿Woe to every slanderer, backbiter﴾ (al-Humazah: 1).

The fourth quality: that he is *mashsha'* with *namim*, i.e., he walks about with tale-bearing among people to cause discord between them. It is said: *namma yanimmu* and *yanunnu*, *namman*, *namiman* and *namimah*.

The fifth quality: that he is *mannaa'* to good. Regarding this there are two views:

One of them: that what is meant is that he is stingy, and "good" means wealth.

The second: he used to prevent his family from good, which is Islam.

This verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. He had ten sons, and he used to say to them and those near them: "If any one of you follows the religion of Muhammad, I will never benefit him with anything." So he prevented them from Islam, and this is the good that he prevented them from. It was reported from Ibn Abbas that it is Abu Jahl. From Mujahid: al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth. From al-Suddi: al-Akhnas ibn Shariq.

The sixth quality: that he is *mu'tadi* (transgressing). Muqatil said: its meaning is that he is a wrongdoer who oversteps and exceeds the truth, so he commits injustice. It is possible to interpret it as encompassing all blameworthy character traits, meaning that he is the extreme in all vileness and disgrace.

The seventh quality: that he is *atheem* (sinful), which is an intensification in sin.

The eighth quality: *'utull*. The opinions of the exegetes regarding it are many, and they are confined to two matters:

One of them: that it is a disparagement of physical form.

The second: that it is a disparagement of character, and it is derived from your saying *'atalahu* when one leads him with violence and harshness. From this is His saying: ﴿Seize him﴾ (al-Dukhan: 47). As for those who understood it as a disparagement of form: Ibn Abbas, in the narration of 'Ata, said: he means strong and bulky. Muqatil said: wide-bellied, robust of build. al-Hasan said: vile in character, base of soul. 'Ubaydah ibn 'Umayr said: he is the great eater and drinker, strong and powerful. al-Zajjaj said: he is coarse and harsh. As for those who understood it as a disparagement of character, they said: he is extremely contentious, harsh and violent.

The ninth quality: His saying: ﴿zanim﴾ (of doubtful lineage). Regarding this there are two issues:

The first issue: regarding *zanim* there are several views:

The first: al-Farra' said: the *zanim* is the claimed one, attached to a people while not being of them. Hassan said:

*"You are a zanim, attached among the family of Hashim, as the single cup is hung behind the rider."*

*Al-zanamah* in anything is an extra part. A goat's *zanamah* is also when its ear is slit, so it becomes loose and dried, and remains like a hanging thing. So the summary is that the *zanim* is the child of fornication who is attached to a people in lineage while not being of them. al-Walid was a claimed one among Quraysh, not of their stock; his father claimed him eighteen nights after his birth. It is also said: his mother committed adultery and he was not known until this verse was revealed.

The second view: al-Sha'bi said: he is the man who is known for evil and baseness, just as a goat is known by its *zanamah*.

The third view: from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: the meaning of his being *zanim* is that he had a *zanamah* on his neck by which he was known. Muqatil said: he had something like a goat's *zanamah* at the base of his ear.

The second issue: His saying *ba'da dhalika* (after that) means that after having enumerated for him these defects and shortcomings, he is *'utull* and *zanim*. This indicates that these two descriptions, namely being *'utull* and *zanim*, are the worst of his faults; for when one is coarse and harsh of nature, his heart hardens and he dares every disobedience. Moreover, the usual case is that when the seed is corrupt, the offspring is corrupt. For this reason the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him said: "The child of fornication will not enter Paradise, nor his offspring, nor the offspring of his offspring." It is also said that here *ba'da dhalika* is like *thumma* in His saying: ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ (al-Balad: 17). al-Hasan read *'utullun* in the nominative as an expression of censure.

The second issue: ﴿fa-yudhinun﴾ is in the nominative and not in the subjunctive by the implied *an*, although it is the answer to the wish (*tamanni*); this is because it has been turned to another way, namely that it is made the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "fa-hum yudhinun" (so they compromise), like His saying: ﴿So whoever believes in his Lord, he fears no ...﴾ (al-Jinn: 13), meaning: "They wish you would compromise, so they compromise then." Sibawayh said: Harun, who was among the reciters, claimed that in some of the codices it reads: "Wadduu law tudhinu fa-yudhinu" (they wish you would compromise, so that they would compromise). Know that when He forbade him to obey the deniers, this includes forbidding obedience to all disbelievers, but He repeated the prohibition against obeying those among the disbelievers who were described with blameworthy qualities beyond disbelief. These qualities are the following:

The first quality: that he is *halaf* (an oft-swearer). The *halaf* is one who swears often, whether in truth or falsehood, and that is enough of a deterrent for one who is accustomed to swearing. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾ (al-Baqarah: 224).

The second quality: that he is *mahin* (contemptible). al-Zajjaj said: it is *fa'il* from *mahana* (contemptibility). Then there are two views:

One of them: that *mahana* is lowliness and insignificance in opinion and discernment.

The second: that he is contemptible because what is meant is one who swears falsely, and a liar is despised by people.

I say: that he is an oft-swearer indicates that he does not know the greatness and majesty of Allah the Exalted, for if he knew that, he would not have proceeded at every time and occasion, for the sake of every falsehood, to call upon His name and attributes as witness. The third quality: that he is *hammaz*, which is the one who defames and reviles. al-Mubarrad said: the one who *yahmiz* people, i.e., reminds them of what is disliked, and the effect of that is revealing faults. One of them: that what is meant is that he is stingy, and "good" means wealth.

The second: he used to prevent his family from good, which is Islam.

This verse was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. As for the second: its implied sense is, "Because he possesses wealth and sons, when Our verses are recited to him, he says, 'The fables of the ancients.'" The meaning is that, because he possesses wealth and sons, he made the recompense for these blessings which Allah bestowed upon him to be disbelief in His verses.

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi (Abu ʿAli al-Fārisī) said: The governing element of His saying ﴿Because he possesses﴾ is either His saying (tutlā, "is recited"), or His saying (qāla, "he says"), or a third thing. The first is invalid, because (tutlā) has been made to be governed by (idhā, "when"), and what is governed by an adjunct cannot govern what precedes it. Do you not see that you do not say, "al-qitāl Zaydan ḥīna ya'tī" meaning "ḥīna ya'tī Zaydan"? Nor is it permissible for it to govern it either; he said: because (qāla) is the answer to (idhā), and the rule of the answer is that it comes after that of which it is the answer, and does not precede it. Since these two divisions are invalid, we know that the governing element is a third thing indicated by what is in the speech, and that is "he denies" or "he disbelieves," or "he refuses to accept the truth," or something similar. The meaning may govern it even though it precedes it, because of its resemblance to an adverb of time, and meanings may govern adverbs even when they precede them. What shows its resemblance to the adverb is the estimate of the lām with it, for the estimate of the verse is: "Because he possesses wealth." When it becomes like an adverb, there is no barrier to the meaning governing it, just as there is no barrier to it governing in His saying: ﴿He will inform you, when you are torn to utter shreds, that indeed you are in a new creation﴾ (Saba: 7), since it is an adverb, and the governing element is the oath indicated by His saying ﴿that indeed you are in a new creation﴾. Likewise His saying ﴿Because he possesses wealth and sons﴾: its estimate is, "that he denied Our verses because he possesses wealth and sons," or "disbelieved in Our verses because he possesses wealth and sons."

The second issue: It is read as (a-an kāna), in the interrogative form, and the estimate is: "Is it because he possesses wealth that he denies?" or the estimate is: "Do you obey him because he possesses wealth?" A parallel to turning the conditional toward the addressee is turning the expectation toward him in His saying: ﴿Perhaps he will be reminded﴾ (Taha: 44).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 68, verse 16:

﴿We shall brand him upon the snout.﴾

Among the issues in this verse:

The first issue: al-Wasm (branding) is the trace of a cauterization or something similar. It is said: "wasamtuhu" (I branded him), so he is "mawsum" (branded) with a mark by which he is recognized, either a burn, or a cut in the ear as a sign for him.

The second issue: al-Mubarrad said: al-Khurtum (snout) here means the nose. This word was used in a manner of contempt toward him, because referring to human organs by names set for the similar organs of animals is a form of disparagement, just as human lips are referred to as al-mashafir (animal lips), and their hands and feet as al-aẓlaf and al-hawafir (hooves).

The third issue: The face is the most honorable place on the body, and the nose is the most honorable part of the face because it rises above it. For this reason they made it the place of honor and zeal, and they derived from it al-anafah (pride/self-respect). They said: "al-anaf fi al-anf" (the nose is in the nose, i.e., pride is in pride) and "hama anfahu" (he protected his nose), and "fulan shamikh al-'irnin" (so-and-so is high-nosed, i.e., proud). And for the humiliated they said: "judi'a anfuhu" (his nose was slit) and "raghima anfuhu" (his nose was rubbed in the dust). So by expressing the branding upon the snout, He conveyed the utmost degree of abasement and humiliation, because a mark upon the face is a disgrace, so how much more upon the most honorable place of the face.

The fourth issue: Some said: this branding will take place in the Hereafter, and some said it will take place in this world.

As for the first view, there are several interpretations:

The first of them, which is the view of Muqatil and Abu al-'Aliyah and the choice of al-Farra': the meaning is that his face will be blackened before entering the Fire. Although the snout has been singled out for the mark, the intended meaning is the face, because part of the face stands for the whole.

The second: God, exalted is He, will place on him in the Hereafter a sign by which the people of the Resurrection will recognize that he was extreme in enmity toward the Messenger and in denying the true religion.

The third: In the verse there is another possibility in my view, which is that this disbeliever only went to extremes in enmity toward the Messenger and in attacking the true religion due to pride and zeal. Since the source of this denial was pride and zeal, the source of the torment of the Hereafter is this same pride and zeal. Thus He expressed this correspondence by His saying: ﴿We shall brand him upon the snout.﴾

As for the second view, that this branding takes place in this world, there are several interpretations:

The first of them: Ibn 'Abbas said: "We shall strike him on the snout with the sword, and make that an enduring mark on his nose for as long as he lives." It is narrated that he fought on the day of Badr and his nose was struck with a sword in the fighting.

The second: The meaning of this branding is that he becomes famous with bad remembrance and an ugly description in the world. The meaning is: We shall attach to him something that will not leave him, and make his matter clear with a manifest clarity so that it is not hidden, just as the brand is not hidden on the snouts of camels. The Arabs say of a man whom they revile with a lasting, ugly, shameful insult: "He has branded him with a brand of evil." The meaning is that He attached to him a shame that does not leave him, just as the brand does not fade or disappear at all. Jarir said:

When I placed my brand upon al-Farazdaq, and upon al-Ba'ith, I slit the nose of al-Akhtal.

He means that he branded al-Farazdaq (and al-Ba'ith) and slit the nose of al-Akhtal with satire, that is, he cast upon him a shame that does not vanish. Without doubt, this great extent of blame upon al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah has remained across the course of time, and so that was like the brand upon the snout. Among what supports this interpretation is the statement of one who said regarding (zanim) that he is known by evil just as the sheep is known by its zanamah (the tuft hanging from its neck).

The third: It is narrated from al-Nadr ibn Shumayl that al-Khurtum is wine, and he recited:

You spend your day in amusement and in pleasure, *** and at night you are a drinker of the khara'tim (the snouts/wine).

According to this, the meaning of the verse is: We shall discipline him for drinking wine, and this is a forced interpretation. It is said that wine is called al-khurtum just as it is called al-sulafah, which is what has passed (salafa) from the juice of the grape, or because it flies (tatir) into the nostrils (khayashim).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 68, verses 17–18:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have tested them as We tested the people of the garden, when they swore that they would surely harvest its fruit in the morning,﴾ ﴿and they did not make an exception.﴾ Know that when the Exalted said, "Because he has wealth and sons," and [the disbelieving man] denied, disbelieved, disobeyed and persisted in rebellion, and this was a question in the form of denial, He made clear in this verse that He had given him wealth and sons only as a trial and a test, and so that he would devote it to obedience to God and would constantly give thanks for the blessings of God. If he did not do that, the Exalted would cut off those blessings from him and pour upon him various kinds of affliction and calamities. So He said: ﴿Indeed, We have tested them as We tested the people of the garden.﴾ That is: We obligated these people to be thankful for the blessings, just as We obligated the people of the garden, the garden with fruit trees, to be thankful and to give the poor their rights. It is narrated that a man from Thaqif, who was a Muslim, owned an estate in which there were palm trees and crops near San'a'. At the harvest he would set aside a generous portion of all its produce for the poor. When he died, his sons inherited it from him. Then they said: "Our dependents are many and the wealth is little, and we cannot give to the needy as our father used to do." So God burned their garden. It was also said that they were among the Children of Israel. His words, ﴿when they swore,﴾ mean: when they took an oath; ﴿that they would surely harvest﴾ means that they would surely cut the fruit of their palm trees; ﴿in the morning﴾ means at the time of morning. Muqatil said: its meaning is, "Go out early in secret to your garden and harvest it, and do not inform the poor." Their father used to inform the poor, and they would gather at the harvesting of his garden. It is said: "He cut the cluster from the palm tree" (qad sarama al-idhq 'an al-nakhlah), and "the palm trees were harvested" (asramma al-nakhl) when the time for its harvest came. His words, ﴿and they did not make an exception,﴾ mean that they did not say, "if God wills." This is the saying of the majority of the commentators (mufassirin). It is said: "So-and-so swore an oath with no exception (thunya) and no reservation (thanwa), no qualification (thaniyya), no reservation (mathnawiyya), and no exception (istithna')," and all of these are one in meaning. The root of all of this is from al-thany (ثني), which means to restrain and to turn back, because when the one swearing says, "By God, I will surely do such-and-such, unless God wills otherwise," he has turned back the binding of that oath. The commentators differed regarding His words, ﴿and they did not make an exception.﴾ The majority say that they did not make an exception by the will of God because they were as those who were confident that they would surely be able to accomplish that. Others said: rather, what is meant is that they would harvest all of it and would not set aside for the poor any part of that amount which their father used to give to the poor.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then a visitation from your Lord swept over it while they were asleep﴾ ﴿so it became like a harvest cut down﴾. "A visitation from your Lord" means a punishment from your Lord. The word *ṭāʾif* is used only for something that comes by night, meaning that a visitor from the punishment of God came upon it. Al-Kalbi said: God sent a fire from the sky upon it, and it burned while they slept, so the garden became like *al-ṣarīm*.

Know that *al-ṣarīm* is on the pattern *faʿīl*, which may be in the sense of the passive participle (*maf‌ʿūl*, "cut off") or in the sense of the active participle (*fāʿil*, "cutting off"). There are several possibilities here:

First: when it burned, it resembled a garden whose fruit has been cut off by destruction of its produce, even though differences arose in other respects. For when trees are burned, they do not resemble trees whose fruit has been cut off. Yet although this difference exists in this respect, the resemblance in the destruction of the fruit is present.

Second: al-Hasan said: the good was cut off from it, so nothing remained in it. On these two readings, *al-ṣarīm* is in the sense of *al-maṣrūm* (the one cut off).

Third: *al-ṣarīm* is a large piece of sand that is cut off from the rest of the sands, and its plural is *al-ṣarāʾim*. On this reading, the garden, while burned with no fruit or good in it, was likened to a sand-heap cut off from the other sands, which produces nothing of use.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 68, verse 28–30:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The best of them said﴾, meaning the most just of them and the most excellent of them. We have already explained its meaning in the commentary on His saying: ﴿a justly balanced community﴾.

﴿Did I not tell you, "Why do you not glorify [God]?"﴾ meaning, "Why do you not glorify [God]?" (lawla, "why not"). There are several interpretations of this:

The first: Most scholars said: its meaning is, "Why do you not make an exception (istithna') saying: If God wills?" For God, exalted is He, only censured them for not making the exception. Then God, exalted is He, answered this statement by saying: ﴿Shall We treat the Muslims like the criminals? What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾

The meaning of the speech is that equating the obedient with the disobedient is not permissible. In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Al-Qadi said: In it there is clear evidence that describing a person as "Muslim" and "criminal" is like a contradiction, so since the sinner is a criminal, he must not be a Muslim. The reply: God denied making the Muslim a likeness of the criminal, and there is no doubt that the intended meaning is not the denial of resemblance in all matters, for the two resemble each other in substance, bodily form, having been created, animality, and many other matters. Rather, the intended meaning is the denial that they are equal in Islam and in criminality, or in the effects of these two matters, or the intended meaning is the denial that the effect of the Muslim's Islam be equal to the effect of the criminal's crime in the sight of God. This is accepted without dispute. So from where does it indicate that one single person cannot be both a Muslim and a criminal?

The second issue: Al-Jubba'i said: The verse indicates that the criminal will absolutely not be in Paradise, because God denied that equality occurs between them. If both were in Paradise, equality would occur between them in reward. Rather, perhaps the criminal's reward would be greater than the Muslim's if the criminal lived longer than the Muslim and his acts of obedience were not nullified.

The answer: This is weak, because we have explained that the verse does not prevent equality from occurring in anything at all, but rather prevents equality from occurring in the degree of reward. Perhaps the two are equal in it, or rather the reward of the Muslim who did not disobey is greater than the reward of the one who disobeyed. Moreover, we say: why is it not permissible that the intended meaning of "the criminals" be the disbelievers whom God related this event about? That is because applying a plural with the definite article (al-) to a previously known referent is well known in language and custom.

The third issue: God denied equality between the Muslims and the criminals in reward, so this indicates that it is rationally ugly (qabuha 'aqlan) what is reported from the People of the Sunnah, that it is permissible for the disbelievers to enter Paradise and the obedient to enter the Fire. The answer: God denied that by way of grace and favor, not because anyone deserves anything from Him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 68, verses 42–44 (part 1 of 2):

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do you have oaths binding upon Us until the Day of Resurrection, that you will have whatever you judge?﴾ On this verse there are two issues:

The first issue: It is said: "So-and-so has a yamin (binding oath/pledge) upon me for such-and-such," when you have guaranteed it to him and sworn to him to fulfil it. The meaning here is: "Or do you have a guarantee from Us, [a pledge] from you, and We have sworn to you with emphatic oaths that reach the utmost in affirmation." If it is asked: "With what does *ilā* (until) in His saying ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ connect?" We say: there are two possibilities.

The first: it connects with His saying ﴿bāligha⁠h⁠ (binding/reaching)﴾, meaning that these oaths are in their strength and completeness such that they reach until the Day of Resurrection.

The second: the sense is "oaths that remain until the Day of Resurrection." Then the meaning of *bāligha* is emphatic, as when you say: "good, exceedingly so" (*jayyida bāligha*). Everything that is perfect in soundness and excellence is *bāligh*. As for His saying ﴿Indeed, for you is what you judge﴾, it is the answer to the oath, because the meaning of ﴿Or do you have oaths upon Us﴾ is "or We have sworn to you."

The second issue: Al-Hasan read *bāligha* in the accusative (*bāligha⁠n*), and it is an accusative of state (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase [of time]. Then He said to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace: ﴿Ask them, which of them stands surety for that?﴾

The meaning is: which of them is a guarantor (*za‘īm*) for that judgement, i.e., who takes responsibility for it and for establishing its soundness by argument, just as the leader (*za‘īm*) of a people takes charge of their affairs.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Or do they have partners? Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful.﴾

Regarding its interpretation there are two views:

The first: the meaning is, "Or do they have things which they believe to be God's partners, so that they believe those partners will make them in the Hereafter like the believers in reward and in deliverance from punishment?" He attributed the partners to them only because they made them partners of God. This is like His saying: ﴿Is there any of your partners who does anything of that?﴾ (al-Rum: 40).

The second view: the meaning is, "Or do they have people who share with them in this doctrine, which is equating the Muslims with the criminals? Then let them bring them, if they are truthful in their claim." The purpose is to show that just as they have no rational proof for establishing this doctrine, nor any transmitted proof, which is a Book they study, so they have no one among the sensible who agrees with them on this view; and that indicates it is false in every respect.

Know that when He, exalted is He, had refuted their claim and corrupted their statement, He then described the greatness of the Day of Resurrection.

So He said: ﴿The Day when a shin will be uncovered﴾, and on this there are several issues:

The first issue: With what is *yawma* (the Day) in the accusative governed? There are three possibilities:

One: it is governed by the verb "then let them bring" in His saying ﴿then let them bring their partners﴾, because that day is a severe day. As if He said: "If they are truthful that they are partners, then let them bring them on the Day of Resurrection, so that they may benefit them and intercede for them."

Second: it is governed by an implied "remember" (*udhkur*).

Third: the sense is "The Day when a shin is uncovered, such-and-such will happen," and it has been omitted for emphatic awe, and because there are among the events [of that day] things which cannot be described because of their greatness.

The second issue: Is this day on which a shin is uncovered the Day of Resurrection, or is it in this world? There are two views:

The first, which is the view of the majority, is that it is the Day of Resurrection. Then, regarding the interpretation of *sāq* (shin/leg), there are several views:

The first: it means severity (*al-shidda*). It is narrated that Ibn ‘Abbas was asked about this verse and he said: "If something of the Qur'an is hidden from you, seek it in poetry, for it is the register (*dīwān*) of the Arabs. Have you not heard the poet's saying:

*Your people have set for us the striking of necks,*
*and war has stood upon us by the shin.*"

Then he said: it means distress and severity. Mujahid narrated from him, saying: it is the most severe hour of the Day of Resurrection. The lexicographers recited many verses, among them:

*"If she has hitched up her skirts for you, by her shin,*
*then, O Rabi‘, 'woe!' and do not weary."*

And among them:

*"She has uncovered for you her shin,*
*and the plain evil has appeared."*

Jarir said:

*"Many a one with lowered gaze from the family of Mazin,*
*when war hitched up its shin, hitched up [his own]."*

Another said:

*"In a year whose shin has been hitched up,*
*a red one, stripping the flesh from its bones."*

Another said:

*"It has hitched up its shin, so tighten [your resolve],*
*and war has pressed upon you, so strive."*

Then Ibn Qutayba said: The origin of this is that when a man falls into a great matter that requires exertion in it, he hitches up his shin. Therefore, it is said in a place of severity: "he uncovered his shin." Know that this is an acknowledgement by the lexicographers that the use of *shin* for severity is figurative (*majāz*). The scholars have agreed that it is not permissible to turn speech to the figurative sense except after the impossibility of taking it in its literal sense (*ḥaqīqa*). So when we establish decisive proofs that it is impossible for Him, exalted is He, to be a body, then it is obligatory to turn the word to the figurative sense.

Know that the author of *al-Kashshaf* presented this interpretation in another context, saying: "Uncovering the shin is a metaphor for the severity of a matter. So the meaning of His saying ﴿The Day when a shin is uncovered﴾ is: the Day when the matter becomes severe and grave, and there is no uncovering there, nor a shin, just as you say of a crippled miser: 'his hand is shackled,' though there is no hand there nor a shackle, and it is only a metaphor for stinginess." Then he began to magnify the science of rhetoric (*‘ilm al-bayān*), saying: "Were it not for it, we would not have come to know these secrets."

I say: either he claims that he turned the word away from its apparent sense without evidence, or he says that this is not permissible except after the impossibility of taking it literally. The first is false by the consensus (*ijmā‘*) of the Muslims, and because if we permit that, the doors of the philosophers' interpretations concerning the Hereafter would be opened, for they say about His saying ﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ (al-Buruj: 11): "There are neither rivers nor trees there; it is only a metaphor for pleasure and happiness." And they say about His saying ﴿Bow and prostrate﴾ (al-Hajj: 77): "There is neither prostration nor bowing there; it is only a metaphor for glorification." And it is known that this leads to abolishing the sacred law and corrupting the religion.

As for if he says that one does not resort to this interpretation except after the establishment of proof that the word cannot be taken in its apparent sense, then this is what every one of the theologians has always held and relied upon, so where are these subtleties which he claims to have exclusively known and understood through the science of rhetoric? So may God have mercy on a man who knows his own measure and does not exceed his limit.

The second view: it is the view of Abu Sa‘id al-Darir: ﴿The Day when a shin is uncovered﴾, that is, the uncovering of the root of the matter. The *sāq* of a thing is its root upon which its stability rests, like the trunk of a tree and the shin of a man. That is, on the Day of Resurrection the realities of things and their roots will be made manifest.

The third view: "The Day when the shin of Hell is uncovered," or "the shin of the Throne," or "the shin of a great and awe-inspiring angel." The wording does not indicate anything except a shin, so whose shin it is, the wording gives no indication of.

The fourth view, which is the choice of the *mushabbiha* (anthropomorphists), is that it is the shin of God, exalted is He above it. It is narrated from Ibn Mas‘ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "He, exalted is He, will manifest Himself to creation on the Day of Resurrection when the Muslims pass by. He will say: 'Whom do you worship?' They will say: 'We worship God.' He will make them witness twice or thrice. Then He will say: 'Do you recognize your Lord?' They will say: 'Glory be to Him! If He makes Himself known to us, we will recognize Him.' At that point He will uncover a shin, and no believer will remain except that he falls down prostrate, while the hypocrites' backs will remain like a single plate, as if there were iron rods in them."

Know that this view is false for several reasons:

One: the proofs have established that every body is originated (*muḥdath*), because every body is finite, and every finite thing is originated; and because every body cannot be free from motion and rest, and whatever is like that is originated; and because every body is contingent (*mumkin*), and every contingent thing is originated.

Two: if that were the intended meaning, it would have been necessary for the shin to be known, because it would be a specific, well-known shin to them, namely the shin of the Merciful. But if we take it to mean severity, then the purpose of the indefinite form is to indicate magnificence, as if it were said: "The Day when severity is uncovered, and what severity!" That is, a severity that cannot be described.

Three: recognition does not come about by uncovering the shin, but by uncovering the face.

The second view: that His saying ﴿The Day when a shin is uncovered﴾ does not refer to the Day of Resurrection, but to this world. This is the view of Abu Muslim, who said: "It is not possible to take it to mean the Day of Resurrection, because He, exalted is He, said in describing that Day: ﴿And they will be called to prostration﴾ (al-Qalam: 42), and on the Day of Resurrection there is no worship or obligation." Rather, it refers either to the last days of a man's life in this world, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day they see the angels, there will be no good news﴾ (al-Furqan: 22); then he sees people being called to the prayers when their times arrive, and he is unable to pray, because it is the time when faith will not benefit a soul. Or it refers to the state of old age, illness, and weakness, when they were previously called to prostration while they were sound of the afflictions they now have, either from the severity that descends upon them from the terror of what they witness at death, or from weakness and old age. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Why then, when it reaches the throat?﴾ (al-Waqi‘a: 83).

Know that there is no dispute that the word can be taken in the sense that Abu Muslim mentioned. As for his statement that it cannot be taken to refer to the Resurrection because the command to prostrate is present here and the obligations cease on the Day of Resurrection, the answer is that this will not be in the manner of obligation, but in the manner of rebuke and humiliation. So why do you say that this is impermissible?

The third issue: It has been read ﴿yawma nakshifu⁠ (We uncover)﴾ with the *nūn*, and ﴿takshifu⁠ (it uncovers)﴾ with an upper dotted *tā’*, both in the active and passive voice. The verb refers to the Hour or to the situation, meaning: "the Day when the situation or the Hour becomes severe," just as you say: "the war uncovered its shin," figuratively. It has also been read ﴿tukshifu⁠ (it uncovers)﴾ with a *tā’* that is vowelled with a *ḍamma* and with the *shīn* vowelled with a *kasra*, from *akshafa*, when one enters into uncovering. From this comes *akshafa al-rajul*, so he is *mukshif*, when his upper lip has been turned up.

* His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will be called to prostration but they will be unable [to do so]. Their eyes will be humbled; humiliation will cover them, and they were being called to prostration while they were sound.﴾

Know that we have made clear that they are not called to prostration as worship and obligation, but as rebuke and reproach for their abandoning prostration in this world. Then, at the very time He calls them to prostration, He removes from them the ability to prostrate and sets a barrier between them and the capacity [to do so], so that their grief and regret over what they neglected will increase, at the very time they were called to prostration while they were sound in their limbs and joints. Al-Jubba'i said: "Since He restricted the lack of capacity to the Hereafter, this indicates that in this world they were able. Thereby the view of those who say that the disbeliever has no capacity to believe, and that the capacity to believe is only acquired when faith exists, is refuted." The answer to him is that God's knowledge that he will not believe is incompatible with the existence of faith, and combining two incompatible things is impossible. So the capacity in this world is also not present according to al-Jubba'i's view.

As for His saying ﴿Their eyes will be humbled⁠﴾, it is a state (*ḥāl*) from the phrase "they are unable." ﴿Humiliation will cover them⁠﴾, meaning: disgrace will befall them because they were not persistent in serving their Master, like a slave whom his master has turned away from; he will be humiliated among people. As for His saying ﴿and they were being called to prostration while they were sound⁠﴾, it means: when they were being called to the prayers by the adhan and the iqama, and they were sound and capable of praying. In this there is a warning for whoever stays away from the congregation and does not respond to the muezzin's call to establish the prayer in congregation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So leave Me with whoever denies this discourse. We will lead them step by step from where they do not know.﴾

Know that when He, Exalted, warned the disbelievers with the magnitude of the Day of Resurrection, He intensified the warning and threatened them with what is with Him of power and subjugation. So He said: ﴿Leave Me with the one who denies this discourse﴾ (dharni wa-iyyahu), meaning: leave him to Me, for I shall suffice you against him. It is as if He says: "O Muhammad, it is enough of retribution against him that you entrust his affair to Me and leave between Me and him, for I know what must be done to him and I am able to do it." Then He said: ﴿We shall draw them on step by step﴾ (sa-nastadrijuhum). It is said: istadraja-hu ila kadha, when one brings him down to it degree by degree until he is ensnared in it. As for His saying ﴿from where they do not know﴾, Abu Rawq said: "﴿We shall draw them on step by step﴾ means: whenever they commit a sin, We renew a blessing for them and cause them to forget seeking forgiveness. So the istidraj occurs only through the prosperity of which they are not aware that it is istidraj, namely the favours bestowed upon them, for they suppose it to be a preference of them over the believers, while in reality it is a cause of their destruction."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 68, verse 50:

There are two issues here.

The first issue: concerning the verse, there are two opinions.

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: God returned revelation to him and granted him intercession for his people.

The second: Some people said: Perhaps he was not a messenger possessing revelation before this incident, and then after this incident God made him a messenger. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿Then his Lord chose him﴾. Those who deny miracles (karamat) and preparatory signs (irhas) must necessarily choose the first opinion, because his being confined in the belly of the fish and his not dying there, when it was not a preparatory sign or a karama, must necessarily be a miracle (mu'jiza), and that requires that he was a messenger in that state.

Page 88

The second issue: The Ash'aris (al-Ashab) argued that the act of the servant is the creation of God, the Exalted, by His words: ﴿So He made him among the righteous﴾. The verse indicates that this righteousness came about only through God's making (ja'l) and creation. Al-Jubba'i said: It is possible that the meaning of "made him" (ja'alahu) is that He informed him of that, and it is possible that He showed him kindness (lataf) so that he became righteous, since "ja'l" is used in the language in these meanings.

The answer: These two opinions you mentioned are metaphorical (majaz), and the basic principle in speech is its literal meaning (haqiqa).

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost slip you with their eyes when they hear the Reminder﴾. Concerning this there are two issues:

The first issue: "in" (in) is the lightened form of the heavy (thaqila) and the lam is its sign.

The second issue: It was recited as ﴿liyuzliqunaka﴾ with a damma and a fatha on the ya, and "zalaqahu" and "azlaqahu" have the same meaning; it is said: "zalaqa al-ra's" and "azlaqahu" meaning he shaved it. It was also recited as "liyuzhiqunaka," from "zahaqat nafsuhu" and "azhaqaha." Then there are opinions regarding it:

The first: They, from the intensity of their staring and their looking at you sideways with eyes of enmity and hatred, almost make your foot slip, from the saying of people: "He looked at me with a look that almost knocks me down" and "almost eats me," meaning that if his look could bring about the knocking down or the eating, he would do it. The poet said:

They exchange, when they meet in a place, glances that remove the footing of feet.

Ibn 'Abbas recited, when he passed by people who sharpened their gaze at him:

They looked at me with reddened eyes, like the look of rams at the knives of the butcher.

God, exalted is He, explained that this look used to intensify from them during the Prophet's ﷺ recitation of the Qur'an, and that is His words: ﴿when they hear the Reminder﴾.

The second: Some of them took it to mean striking by the evil eye (al-'ayn). Here there are two positions:

The first: Striking by the evil eye, is it in general a real thing or not?

The second: Assuming that it is valid, is the verse here explained by it or not?

The first position: Some people denied this and said: The influence of one body on another is only conceivable through contact, and here there is no contact, so the occurrence of influence is impossible.

Know that the first premise is weak. For a human being is either the soul or the body. If it is the first, there is no impossibility in the souls differing in their substances and quiddities, and if that is so, there is also no impossibility in their differing in their properties and effects, so it is not far-fetched that some souls have a special property of influence. If it is the second, there is also no impossibility in a person's temperament being arranged in a particular way that has a special effect. In sum, the rational possibility stands, and there is not even a doubt, let alone a proof, in its falsehood. And the textual evidences (sam'iyya) speak to this, as it is related that he, peace be upon him, said: "The evil eye is real," and said: "The evil eye brings a man into the grave and a camel into the cooking pot."

The second position: Some people interpreted the verse in this sense. They said: The evil eye was among the Banu Asad, and a man among them would go hungry for three days, then nothing would pass by him, and he would say about it: "I have not seen the like of today," except that he would afflict it with the evil eye. So the disbelievers asked one of those who had this quality to say that about the Messenger of God ﷺ, but God, exalted is He, protected him. Al-Jubba'i criticized this interpretation and said: Striking by the evil eye arises from admiring a thing, and the people were not looking at the Messenger, peace be upon him, in this manner; rather they were hating and detesting him, and looking in this way does not necessitate striking by the evil eye.
